title: CRAFT: The Prompt Engineering Framework That Every Tech-Professional Needs
partialText:
The CRAFT Framework for Effective Prompt Engineering
Most people, including tech professionals, often use AI sub-optimally due to poor communication and vague problem descriptions. To address this, the CRAFT Framework provides a memorable and effective structure for creating high-quality AI prompts, delivering consistent results across contexts and domains.

CRAFT Framework Overview
C - Context & Role: Define the AI's persona and the situation in detail (e.g., expertise, industry, goals, constraints).
R - Request & Reason: Clearly specify the task and its goal, starting with an action verb.
A - Augment: Guide the AI with examples and chain-of-thought reasoning to improve accuracy and reduce errors.
F - Format & Fences: Set the structure for the output and define boundaries for data.
T - Trust Boundaries: Include constraints, negative instructions, and guardrails to ensure reliable and safe outputs.

title: How AI Quietly Changed Modern UX Patterns
partialText: Software interaction changed more in the last two years than in the decade before — and most people didn't notice. The article maps the UX patterns that quietly took over: input became intentional (slash commands, selection-based actions, contextual suggestions instead of blank prompts); output became editable instead of regenerate-and-replace; AI moved to where work already happens (Copilot in code, Figma on canvas, Notion in docs); errors turned into conversations rather than dead ends; voice finally became operational; agents started navigating UIs on behalf of users; autonomy turned into a progression (human in/on/over/out of the loop); interfaces became generative and on-demand; and context emerged as the primary design material. The underlying shift: software is moving from task-driven to intent-driven, and design work is moving from static flows to systems that interpret intent, expose the right controls, and maintain trust under increasing autonomy.

title: pytest-conversational Earns a 57 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building a Multi-Turn Chatbot and LLM Agent Testing Plugin
partialText: pytest-conversational is a lightweight open-source pytest plugin designed for testing multi-turn chatbots and LLM agents. Created by Mikhail Golikov, the tool models conversations as sequences of turns and assertions, allowing developers to test Telegram bots and HTTP webhook adapters using familiar pytest workflows. With growing GitHub traction, community pull requests, and planned PyPI support, the project aims to bring standardized QA infrastructure to the rapidly expanding AI agent ecosystem.

title: ZSoftly Cloud Platform (ZCP) Earns a 60.09 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building a Sovereign Canadian Cloud
partialText: ZSoftly Cloud Platform (ZCP) is a newly launched sovereign Canadian cloud built for organizations seeking an alternative to US-owned hyperscalers. Running from Montréal and Ottawa, ZCP offers VMs, Kubernetes, object storage, and observability on open-source infrastructure with predictable CAD pricing and zero egress fees. The platform targets businesses prioritizing data sovereignty, compliance, and freedom from VMware licensing costs and hyperscaler lock-in.

title: three.ws Earns a 78.1 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building Embeddable 3D AI Agents
partialText: three.ws is building open-source infrastructure for embodied AI on the web. The platform lets developers attach LLMs to 3D avatars, register them on-chain, and embed them anywhere using a simple web component. Powered by technologies like Three.js, Solana, Claude, and OpenAI, three.ws aims to become the default infrastructure layer for persistent AI agents with memory, voice, identity, and ownership across the open web.

title: Outdo Earns a 67 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building a Real-Time Competitive Productivity App
partialText: Outdo is a gamified productivity app where friends compete on live leaderboards by completing real-world tasks. After launching in May 2026, Outdo reached 130 users organically in its first week, generating strong engagement through viral sharing and multiplayer task rooms.

title: RoastRocket Earns a 37 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building a 10-Minute Startup Idea Stress-Tester

title: The Email Problem That Kills M&A Deals Is Not the One Anyone Is Watching

title: How I Aligned Years of Time-Lapse Photos With OpenCV and Neural Matching
partialText:
In the previous post, I described the Seasons project: a time-lapse of hundreds of pictures taken from nearly the same viewpoint over the years. The hardest challenge wasn’t taking the pictures or assembling them, but aligning them.

You might have noticed the nearly part about viewpoint in the above paragraph. Indeed, it’s an approximation. I’m a human being, not a tripod. The position changes ever so slightly, and so does the exact angle. My phone has changed over the years, from a Samsung S10 to an S21, and now I’m using an iPhone 14 Pro. Each of them has a different camera with a different focal length. The resulting photos look similar but are definitely not identical: slightly different scales and angles. Without any correction, the landscape appears to be moving a lot.

Alignment is the process of warping each photo so it looks like it was taken from exactly the same angle as a reference image.

title: The Last Mile Problem in Agentic AI: Why Context Abstraction Is the Next Developer Battleground
partialText: AI agents fail when they rely on brittle, hand-written API wrappers. MCP fixes this by giving models a standard way to discover tools and fetch structured live data, so developers spend less time on integration plumbing and more time shipping features.

title:
Markets Don't Move Linearly — They Transition
Between Behavioral States
partialText: Using 38 years of EUR/USD data, this article explores how markets shift between recurring behavioral regimes such as compression, expansion, acceleration, exhaustion, and transition. Through phase-space reconstruction, volatility analysis, and nonlinear modeling, the study suggests that markets may behave less like random walks and more like adaptive systems with changing internal structures.

title: AI Doesn't Exist, and Poop Proves It
partialText: Maybe AI is not artificial intelligence. Maybe it is accumulated intelligence: human thought, language, code, memory, bias, and culture compressed into machines and reflected back at us.
